extracted.intended_audience: chemists, experimental natural philosophers, and laboratory students (historical/Practical chemistry audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and observational guidance for preparing, purifying, concentrating, naming, and studying various organic (vegetable) acids and their salts (e.g., pyro-muqueux, oxalic, acetic, succinic, benzoic, camphoric, gallique, lactique). Emphasis on distillation conditions, oxidation methods, purification techniques, solubility behavior, and nomenclature of resulting salts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation conditions for acids from sugar or sweet bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain pyro-muqueux acid (and similar acids) from sugar and sweet bodies by distillation, distil 'à feu nud' (naked fire) and leave seven eighths of the retort empty because these substances swell greatly with heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distill slowly and with a moderate degree of fire to avoid the evolution of gas; a slow, moderate distillation prevents almost any gas passage. Rectification by a second distillation reduces colour. Beware: some have advised rectifying further, but the Académiciens de Dijon found that rectification of this acid can be dangerous and may cause explosion. The acid is yellowish-reddish and contains mainly water and a small portion of slightly oxygenated oil; it stains the skin yellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrating volatile acids by freezing (cold separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate volatile, water-rich acids by exposing them to freezing temperatures or artificial cold so that the aqueous part freezes and the acid remains liquid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For acetic (vinegar) acid, expose to a cold 4–6 degrees below the freezing point: the aqueous part freezes and the acid remains liquid. This method concentrates without altering the acid's nature, unlike distillation which may change the acid. The same cold-concentration approach is recommended as the best means to concentrate acetic acid without altering it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectification (second distillation) to reduce colour
rubrics_metrics.description: A second distillation (rectification) can be used to obtain a less coloured fraction of an acid obtained by initial distillation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to pyro-muqueux acid: rectifying by a second distillation yields a less coloured acid. However, rectification may be hazardous for some acids (see warning about explosions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxidation of sugar to prepare oxalic acid
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxidize sugar with nitric acid to produce oxalic acid: pour six to eight parts of nitric acid onto part sugar and heat gently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lively effervescence and abundant nitrous gas will be evolved; upon resting the liquor crystals of very pure oxalic acid form. Dry these crystals on gray paper to remove remaining nitric acid and optionally redissolve in distilled water and recrystallize for higher purity. Note: the same oxidative liquor also contains malic acid upon cooling; further oxidation converts sugar into acetic acid (vinegar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of oxalic acid from plant juices (oseille/sorrel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain oxalic acid from expressed sorrel juice; crystals form after long rest, but this natural product may be partly saturated with vegetable fixed alkali (potash).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain pure acid from this material, one must form it artificially (oxidize sugar) or purify the natural product by recrystallization to remove excess alkali.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying and purification procedure for oxidation-produced acids
rubrics_metrics.description: After crystallization from oxidizing reactions, dry crystals on gray paper to separate traces of residual oxidizing acid, and recrystallize from distilled water for added purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: oxalic acid crystals should be dried on a gray paper to remove nitric acid, then dissolved in distilled water and crystallized a second time for greater purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing acetic (vinegar) radical by fermentation and distillation
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce acetic acid (acid acéteux or vinegar) by exposing wine to a mild temperature with a ferment (often existing lees from prior vinegar); barrel should be half full to allow necessary air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spirituous portion (carbon and hydrogen) oxygenates only in open air, accompanied by a diminution of air volume, hence the barrel must be half full. The formed acid is very volatile and greatly diluted with water and foreign substances; distill gently in stone or glass vessels to obtain purer acid. Note that distillation does not fully remove foreign phlegm and may change the acid's nature between distillate and residue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical oxidation routes to acetic acid
rubrics_metrics.description: Acetic acid can be produced chemically by oxidizing tartaric, oxalic, or malic acids with nitric acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, such oxidations may change the proportions of base principles in the radical; further experiments are needed to confirm exact relationships. Hassenfratz was reported to be repeating such experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of 'vinaigre radical' (concentrated acetic acid) from acetites
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare concentrated 'vinaigre radical' by treating an acetite (e.g., acetite of potash or acetite of copper) with one-third of its weight of concentrated sulfuric acid and distilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a very concentrated vinegar called the radical vinegar or acetic acid; but it remains to be decisively proven whether this acid is more oxygenated than ordinary acéteux (acetic) acid or only differs by proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overheating during sublimation/distillation of succinic acid
rubrics_metrics.description: When procuring succinic acid by distillation of succin/amber, use a gentle heat and avoid pushing the distillation too far to prevent passing the oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Succinic acid sublimes as a concrete in the neck of the retort. After operation, let the salt drain on gray paper and purify by repeated dissolution and crystallization. Expect succinic acid to require 24 parts cold water to remain in solution but to be much more soluble in hot water; it is a weak acid and only weakly alters plant blue dyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification by draining on gray paper and repeated recrystallization
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining salts or acidic concretes by distillation or extraction, allow them to drain on gray paper and purify by repeated dissolutions and crystallizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for succinic acid and oxalic procedures; drying on gray paper also used to remove traces of acids like nitric acid from crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metals must be oxygenated to dissolve in vegetable acids
rubrics_metrics.description: For vegetable acids (acetic, tartaric, oxalic, etc.) to dissolve metals, the metals must first be oxygenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a general requirement for the formation of salts with these acids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraction of benzoic acid from benjoin by alkaline digestion and acidification
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract benzoic acid by digesting powdered benjoin in lime (lime water) repeatedly until lime no longer neutralizes, concentrate the combined liquors by evaporation, cool and then add muriatic (hydrochloric) acid dropwise until no further precipitate forms; the precipitate is benzoic acid concret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wet-extraction technique (Schéele's procedure) contrasts with sublimation and is recommended for producing benzoic acid concret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxygeneation of camphor to yield camphoric acid
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxygenate camphor by repeated distillation with nitric acid (Kosegarten reported up to eight times) to convert camphor into an acid close to oxalic acid (camphoric acid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed products suggest camphoric acid may be a mixture of oxalic and malic acids; many phenomena of its combinations with bases mirror those of oxalic and malic acids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraction of gallic (gallique) acid from galls
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain gallic acid by simple infusion or decoction of galls in water, or by distillation at very gentle heat; the Commissioners of the Academy of Dijon studied many of its combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gallic acid reddens litmus, decomposes sulfides, unites with all metals when those metals have been previously dissolved by another acid and precipitates them in various colours (iron gives a blue or deep violet precipitate). Found widely in many plants; its radical is unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect differences in solubility and crystallizability among salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Different organic-acid salts differ markedly in solubility and ability to crystallize: many acétites (first-degree acetous salts) are not crystallizable, whereas salts of tartaric and oxalic acids are generally poorly soluble and crystallize readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malates have solubility intermediate between oxalates and acetates, reflecting intermediate degree of oxygenation of their acid radicals. This informs choice of purification and isolation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of systematic nomenclature for salts (new vs. old nomenclature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the new nomenclature for naming salts of oxygenated radicals (e.g., acetate, oxalate, succinate, benzoate, camphorate, gallate, lactate) while noting ancient/older names and usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides parallel 'Nomenclature nouvelle' and 'Nomenclature ancienne' tables for acéteux/acétique and acétite salts, and notes how many of these combinations were unknown to ancient chemists; the author remarks on historical names and the modern names proposed (examples given throughout the tables).
